description_full: FedEx Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides transportation, e-commerce, and business services in the United States and internationally. The company operates through two segments, Express U.S. Domestic and Express International. It provides e-commerce and digital solutions; dataworks; printing and shipping management, including digital printing, professional finishing, document creation, design solutions, direct mail, signs and graphics, custom-branded boxes, copying, computer rental, Wi-Fi, corporate print solutions, shredding, U.S. passport processing and renewal, and digital notarization; packing services, as well as packing supplies and boxes; document and business services; and retail access for package transportation. In addition, the company offers logistics services, air and ocean cargo transportation, specialty transportation, customs brokerage, trade management tools and data, and door-to-door solutions; and third party logistics and supply chain management solutions, such as inbound logistics, warehousing and distribution, fulfillment, contract packaging and product configuration, systems integration, returns process and disposition, test, repair, refurbishment, and product liquidation. Further, it provides sales, marketing, administrative, information technology, and back-office support services. FedEx Corporation was founded in 1971 and is headquartered in Memphis, Tennessee.
ceo_bio: Mr. Rajesh  Subramaniam | President, CEO & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $16.6M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 300K people. Revenue per employee of $316K ranks in the below the sector median among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 6%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $17K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $590 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 53× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: FedEx Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $75.9B market cap on $94.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $5.1B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.6×.
Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 6.3% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $16.3M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 10% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Valued at a 38% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
23 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.52x).
It accounts for 2.4% of sector revenue and 1.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-8.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 37% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $416.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 6% below its DCF fair value of $343, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $269 to $444 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 17.5 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 8.2 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 14.8 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 57% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 26 covering analysts target $357 on average, 10% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.01x.
ROE of 14% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.1x net debt to EBITDA ($13.3B of cash against $24.0B of debt), with interest covered 5.6x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.7% over 3 years, 2.4% over 5 years and 6.5% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 9.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 4.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 6.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 83%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $16.3M sold).
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (1.0% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years, raising it 14.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 300,000 employees, each generates about $316K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 6.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $17K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $16.6M (53x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
